title: The Inclusion SHIFT
author: Cassie Puplett
summary: Cassie Puplett, headteacher of Lingfield primary school in Surrey, describes how five years of work turned inclusion from SEND support delivered by individual teaching assistants into a whole-school culture. After post-Covid pressures exposed weak systems, the school codified behaviour, routines and communication in a Culture Deck and shared handbooks, which became the foundation for everything else. Its guiding question changed from what support a child gets to what needs the child and family have and what the school can do collectively. She credits early identification in pre-school and Reception, a flexible needs-led provision called The Willows, one-page pupil overviews, and a connected curriculum with shared pedagogy such as Rosenshine and WalkThrus. Inclusion, she insists, must never lower the ceiling, and the shift moved the school from labels to needs, from firefighting in Year 6 to early identification, and from SEND as an add-on to inclusion running through everything.
points: Inclusion is built on five elements the school summarises as Systems, High expectations, Insight, Flexibility and Together.
The guiding question moved from what support a child receives to what needs the child and family have and what the school can collectively do.
Behaviour systems came first and then led the school into policies, professional development, curriculum and assessment, so improvement was iterative rather than a grand plan.
Inclusion must not lower the ceiling, so pupils work toward the same curriculum endpoints with thoughtful adaptations.
Making inclusion everyone's responsibility, with visible pupil overviews and codified consistencies, replaced reliance on the SENCO or one-to-one assistants.
quotes: Our question gradually shifted from “What support does this child get?” to “What needs does this child and their family have, and what can we collectively do about it?
Perhaps the biggest shift, however, has been recognising that inclusion cannot sit solely with the SENCO, DSL, me as Head, or a specialist team.

All too often implementation fails because people are left behind or not enough time is given to ensure its success. Sometimes too many new things lead to initiative fatigue - that doesn’t work either.

All this matters because inclusion should never mean lowering the ceiling. Our ambition is for children to work towards the same curriculum endpoints wherever possible, with thoughtful adaptations that enable them to get there.

We codify this through our everyday systems: our Monday Briefing, Staff Handbook, Agreed Consistencies Handbook, Curriculum Unit Overviews and Bread and Butter planning documents. None of these is particularly exciting on its own, but together they make expectations visible, reduce ambiguity and help us stay aligned.
Inclusion has to remain responsive because children, families and communities change. What worked five years ago won’t necessarily be what our children or families need five years from now.
